title: T-GINEE: Multilayer Networks with Tensor Decomposition
one_liner: A method for analyzing networks with multiple relationship types by sharing latent factors across layers instead of treating each layer separately.
lead: Real-world networks are not simple—they have many different relationship types. A social network has friendship links, family links, and colleague links all at once. Traditional methods either ignore all but one type or just average them together, missing the key fact that different layers depend on each other. This paper builds a system that discovers and models those dependencies.

paras: A real network often has many types of connections. A person on social media might be connected via friendship links, shared interests, geographic proximity, and employer links—all at the same time. Each relationship type forms a separate layer in what is called a multilayer network.

A naive approach is to analyze each layer alone: ignore friendship links and predict from interests only, then ignore interests and predict from geography only. But this is wasteful—if friendship and geographic closeness are correlated, using that fact should help predictions in both layers. Another naive approach is to collapse all layers into one by averaging or summing. But averaging destroys the distinct structure of each layer and loses the ability to say which layers actually depend on each other.
The problem is that no existing method systematically discovers and models how layers actually influence each other. So predictions remain weak and the network structure stays opaque.

callout.html: Share latent factors (hidden explanatory features) across layers so that the layers jointly reveal each other's structure.

steps.b: Encode each layer as a table
steps.text: Store the adjacency (connection strength) between nodes in each layer in a rectangular table of numbers.
Break each layer's table into products of smaller factors—some factors repeat across layers, some are unique.
Use a working covariance table (a table of correlation numbers) to measure how changes in one layer co-vary with changes in another.

steps.b: Fit to data using generalized estimation
steps.text: Iteratively nudge the factors to minimize a combined loss that penalizes mispredictions and incoherence.
The learned factors reveal latent structure; the covariances reveal which layers reinforce or oppose each other.

object.h2: What the paper changes: latent factors
paras: The paper changes how latent factors (hidden features that explain the network structure) are learned. Instead of learning separate factors for each layer, T-GINEE learns factors that can appear in multiple layers at once. A single latent factor might capture why people are friends and why they share interests, because both tend to arise from the same cause: working in the same company or sharing a hobby.

hidden.name: Inter-layer correlation structure
paras: The hidden quantity is how strongly each layer's connections co-move with every other layer's connections. If the friendship layer and the geography layer tend to have strong connections between the same pairs of nodes, their correlation is high. If they are nearly independent, their correlation is near zero.

T-GINEE estimates this correlation using a working covariance matrix (a table where entry [i,j] measures how the i-th and j-th layers behave together). The paper then uses this matrix in the estimation process to nudge the factors so that layers with high correlation share more latent factors, while uncorrelated layers develop unique factors.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger correlation between layers; diagonal high (each layer correlated with itself).

reads.html: Layers that often connect the same pairs of nodes have high correlation. The working covariance table measures this for every pair of layers.

The generalized estimating equation framework uses the working covariance matrix to model how disturbances (prediction errors) in one layer affect disturbances in another, allowing information to flow across layers during fitting.

mechanism.h2: Why sharing factors works: forcing alignment
paras: When two layers share a latent factor, that factor must explain both layers well. This constraint forces the method to find factors that capture genuinely shared structure. If friendship and geography happen to align (same people are both geographically close and friends), a shared factor will emerge to explain both—because a single underlying feature such as 'shared workplace' naturally explains both types of connection. If they do not align, the method will create separate factors because forcing them to share would increase error.

The working covariance matrix guides this process by measuring the actual co-variance in the data. If two layers co-vary strongly in the data, the loss function will penalize them for having different factors, nudging the method toward factor sharing. If they do not co-vary, sharing factors is not forced, so they remain distinct. In this way, the method discovers which layers are really coupled and which are independent, all from the data alone.

stages.s: Raw multilayer network: five adjacency tables
Break tables into shared and unique factors
Compute working covariance from current factors
Measure prediction error and factor misalignment
Shared latent factors + inter-layer correlation table

math.h2: The loss function combines prediction and covariance
math.words: Task loss plus generalized estimating penalty: the prediction error on each layer, plus a penalty that rewards layers for sharing factors when their co-variation in the data is high.
math.equation: L = sum_layer ( prediction_error_layer ) + penalty * sum_pairs ( (factor_diff_ij) * working_cov_ij )
symbols: how wrong the reconstructed layer is from the real data
how much the latent factors differ between layers i and j
measured co-variation between layers i and j in the data
scaling constant controlling how much to reward alignment

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose layers 1 and 2 have working_cov = 0.8 (highly correlated in data).
If they share a factor perfectly, factor_diff = 0, penalty term = 0 * 0.8 = 0 (no penalty).
If factors differ slightly (diff = 0.2), penalty term = 0.2 * 0.8 = 0.16 (small penalty).
For uncorrelated layers with working_cov = 0.1, the same factor_diff = 0.2 gives penalty = 0.2 * 0.1 = 0.02 (tiny penalty).
Result: the method will force shared factors for highly correlated layers but allow divergence for independent ones.

math.note: The working covariance matrix acts as a data-driven mask: pair-wise penalties are strong only when the data itself shows that two layers move together.

bars.h2: Prediction accuracy on a social network

charts.title: Naive: each layer alone
charts.note: Each layer has only partial information, so accuracy is low.

charts.title: T-GINEE: shared factors
charts.note: When layers share factors, information flows between them: a latent factor explaining the friendship layer also explains related structure in the interest and geographic layers (because these layers co-vary in the data), so the method reconstructs all three more accurately.

items.html: Forcing factor sharing on uncorrelated layers damages fit. But T-GINEE protects against this: the working covariance will be near zero, so the penalty for different factors is negligible.

items.b: If one layer is much noisier than others.
items.html: Shared factors may be pulled by noise in a single layer. The paper addresses this by using a task-specific loss function that can down-weight unreliable layers.

items.b: If the number of latent factors is misspecified.
items.html: Too few factors and you cannot capture structure; too many and you overfit. The paper does not provide an automatic method to choose this number.

T-GINEE discovers the true correlation structure because the working covariance guides factor sharing only where the data shows real co-movement, so predictions improve on layers that actually depend on each other, while independent layers evolve their own factors without interference.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A small runnable demo would create a synthetic social network with five layers: friendship, shared interests, geographic proximity, employer affiliation, and hobby group membership. The first three layers would be strongly correlated in the data (people with shared interests tend to live near each other and be friends); the last two would be nearly independent of the first three. A demo would then run T-GINEE, extract the working covariance matrix, and show that it correctly identifies high correlation between the first three layers and low correlation with layers four and five. To prove that shared factors improve prediction, it would measure the error of T-GINEE versus layer-by-layer analysis. Because shared factors allow each layer to use information from correlated layers, T-GINEE should make fewer errors on the first three layers.
demo.closing: The demo must show that the working covariance matrix correctly reflects which layers actually co-vary in the data. It must also show that on correlated layer pairs, T-GINEE has lower prediction error because shared factors let each layer borrow structure from the other.
